noticing_prompts: Photograph the place where you charge your phone. Include the device, cables, furniture, wall, and whatever else is normally there.
Document the inside of a bag you use often, exactly as it is right now. Don’t rearrange it first.
Save a screenshot of an interface you use every week. Keep enough context that someone can tell what task it helped you do.
Photograph your junk drawer, medicine cabinet, nightstand, desk corner, or another small everyday ecosystem before touching anything.
Keep one receipt from an unremarkable purchase and add one sentence about why you bought what you bought.
Record thirty seconds of a sound you usually filter out: a crossing signal, refrigerator hum, transit announcement, laundry machine, hallway, or ventilation system.
Document the route from your front door to the place where you normally put your keys, bag, shoes, or coat.
Photograph something you repaired, improvised, taped together, repurposed, or simply learned to live with.
Write down the tabs, apps, or windows open while you do an ordinary task. Interfaces are environments too.
Document everything within arm’s reach from where you are sitting. No rearranging.
Save a piece of bureaucracy: a form, ticket, confirmation screen, queue number, reminder, notice, or letter that quietly structures your day.
Describe one object you would never think to put in a museum. That’s probably a useful place to start.
Photograph the contents of your refrigerator door, bathroom counter, entryway, or kitchen sink at an ordinary moment.
Record a minute of an ordinary commute or trip: what you see, hear, wait for, tap, scan, carry, or ignore.
Save a notification or settings screen you expect will look completely normal to you in five years.
Document a small routine you do without thinking: making coffee, locking up, feeding an animal, taking medication, charging devices, or getting ready for bed.
Photograph an object twice: once by itself, and once where it normally lives.

questions: what is the museum of ordinary life
what is museum of ordinary life
what kind of museum is this
why is there a museum of ordinary life
entries.answer: The Museum of Ordinary Life is an archive established in 2026. It documents ordinary objects, rooms, interfaces, routines, paperwork, sounds, stories, and the context around them while that context can still be recorded. For now, it’s a distributed digital archive rather than a single building.

questions: what is the point of this museum
why should anyone care about ordinary life
entries.answer: Much of ordinary life disappears without leaving much of a record. Bedrooms, receipts, routines, interfaces, clutter, workarounds, waiting, maintenance, and small habits are easy to lose. The Museum records them before we know which details people will later wish somebody had saved. A life doesn’t have to be exceptional to matter.

questions: why does the collection start in 2026
entries.answer: Because 2026 is when the Museum started. The collection begins in the present instead of trying to reconstruct ordinary context after it has already disappeared.

questions: what can go in the museum
what kinds of things do you collect
can anything be in the museum
what kind of stuff do you want
would this belong in the museum
entries.answer: Almost anything can count if it helps explain how everyday life worked. The Museum is interested in the thing and its context: what it was, where it lived, how it was used, who used it, and when. Rarity, beauty, and a profound story aren’t requirements.

questions: what sections are in the collection
give me examples of what you collect
entries.answer: The current collection categories are Home, Work, Money, Technology, Public life, Paperwork, Routine, and Digital traces. They’re starting points, not strict boxes.
keywords: home work money technology public paperwork routine digital

questions: how do i document ordinary life
how do i take a museum photo
how should i photograph an object
how much context should i include
entries.answer: Keep the thing and its surroundings together. One useful method is to photograph an object twice: once clearly, then again where it normally lives. Save interfaces before they disappear. Don’t worry about making the record profound. A fragment can be useful without explaining a whole person.

how to add something to the museum
okay how do i send something

entries.answer: Send the original photo, video, audio file, screenshot, or document when possible. Tell us what it is and when you documented it. Add an approximate location if it matters and whatever context you want preserved. Then choose publication and reuse permissions separately.

questions: what file types can i send
what kind of files do you accept
can i send you a picture
entries.answer: The site currently asks for original photos, videos, audio files, screenshots, or documents when possible. If what you want to preserve doesn’t fit those forms, contact the Museum rather than forcing it into the wrong format.
keywords: photo video audio screenshot document file

questions: why do you want the original file
should i send the original photo
can i send an edited image
can i send a resized image
should i edit my photo first
entries.answer: The Museum prefers the original file or record when possible because it preserves more of the record. Public copies may later be cropped, resized, or redacted while the archival original is kept separately.

questions: what do i say about my contribution
when should i say it was made
entries.answer: At minimum, say what the thing or record is and when you documented it. The Museum also asks for an approximate location when it matters and any context you want to keep with the record.

questions: do i need to give my location
do i have to say where it is
entries.answer: Give an approximate location only if it matters to the record. A city name is plenty. The contribution instructions do not ask for a precise street address.

questions: how much context do i need
do i need to explain it
what should i write about it
entries.answer: Add as much or as little context as feels right. One sentence can be enough. No explanation can also be useful information. Context might include where something lived, how it was used, what surrounded it, or what it meant to you.

questions: can i choose whether it is public
entries.answer: Submitting something to the archive doesn’t automatically make it public. Preservation and publication are separate. You can allow public display now, choose a later release, ask the Museum to check with you again, or preserve the record without public display.

questions: do i have to use my name
can i contribute without my name
entries.answer: Yes. The current permission model allows public display with your name or anonymously. Attribution for other permitted uses is also recorded separately.

questions: can you publish it in ten years
can i choose a release date
can i keep it closed for years
entries.answer: You can choose a delayed release. The current options include publication on or after a chosen date, waiting a chosen number of years, asking again later, or keeping the record archive-only.

questions: can you preserve it but not publish it
can i submit something that never goes public
can it stay private in the archive
entries.answer: Yes. A contribution can be preserved without public display. The current contribution choices include “archive only and ask before publishing” and “archive only; don’t publish.” Archive-only status doesn’t automatically grant research, machine learning, or generative-reuse permission.

questions: can i require new permission later
what if i am not sure yet
entries.answer: You can require the Museum to ask again after a date or number of years. An “ask again” instruction still requires a new yes before the Museum takes that action.

questions: does public mean research is allowed
can my record be used for research
entries.answer: Research is a separate permission. Public display doesn’t automatically allow research, and archive-only status doesn’t automatically allow it either. You can allow or decline research use separately.

questions: can ai train on my contribution
can my contribution be used for machine learning
do you train ai on submissions
does public mean ai can use it
entries.answer: Machine learning is a separate permission. A contributor may allow or decline computational analysis or learning from the record. Permission for machine learning does not automatically allow generative reuse.

questions: can ai generate from my contribution
can a model remix my work
can my contribution be used to generate things
entries.answer: Generative reuse is recorded separately from machine learning. It covers reproduction, remixing, imitation, or generation from a contribution. Saying yes to machine learning does not automatically mean yes to generative reuse.

questions: can you keep my name only in the archive
entries.answer: Identity and attribution are recorded separately. Reuse can identify the contributor, remain anonymous, or keep attribution only inside the archive, depending on the contributor’s choice.

questions: what if a future use does not exist yet
can you ask me about new uses later
uses that cannot be described yet
entries.answer: For a use that can’t yet be described concretely, the contributor can allow it, decline it, or require the Museum to ask again.

questions: can i delete my record later
entries.answer: Contributors may revise permissions or request withdrawal where the Museum can lawfully and technically do so. Some downstream copies, indexes, or completed model training can’t necessarily be reversed; when that’s true, the Museum says so plainly.

questions: can i submit someone else's personal info
entries.answer: Check files for private information you don’t want preserved, and don’t send private information about another person without permission. Public copies may be redacted while the archival original is kept separately.

entries.answer: Nothing you type into this Help Desk is sent anywhere in the current version. Matching happens in your browser using the Help Desk file already loaded with the page. Reloading the page forgets the conversation.

No. Not yet. This version is a small local question matcher. It reads the Museum’s Help Desk file in your browser and returns the closest curated answer. If the Museum later adds a model, the interface should say so clearly.

questions: can i help run the museum
who takes care of the collection
entries.answer: The Museum is being built around shared stewardship rather than a permanent central curatorial authority. Stewards may care for collections, review records, make exhibitions, document ordinary life, maintain the website and preservation systems, and take part in decisions about context, consent, and interpretation.

questions: how do i become a steward
how can i help the museum
can i help with the archive
entries.answer: The Museum is looking for an initial group of stewards. Participation can begin with one conversation or gathering; there’s no requirement to make an ongoing commitment. Stewardship can include collection work, consent and ethics, interpretation, exhibitions, community work, infrastructure, or translation.

questions: can my community start a museum
can i start a local collection
can there be more than one museum
how does the distributed network work
can we make our own museum
can my neighborhood make one of these
can we make one of these
can my community make one of these
entries.answer: The Museum may take many local forms. A neighborhood, town, language community, diaspora, workplace, or temporary group can keep its own collection and still connect to the wider Museum. Local stewards decide what to collect, how to describe it, which languages to use, and what stays local, closed, delayed, or offline.

questions: does a local museum need a building
do we need a physical museum
can a museum be one day
does this need a permanent space
entries.answer: No building is required. A local museum can be permanent or temporary, physical or digital, and can exist for a day, a season, one question, or one exhibition.

questions: what would a local museum url look like
can we get a museumofordinarylife address
entries.answer: Participating museums may eventually use recognizable addresses within the wider Museum while keeping their own name, languages, collections, exhibitions, and stewards. The site presents this as a possible network structure rather than a finished service.

questions: is this only in san francisco
can people outside the us contribute
is this only for people in america
can people in other countries contribute
is this just a us project
entries.answer: The Museum isn’t limited to one city or country. Records can come from anywhere ordinary life is being lived and documented, and communities anywhere may establish their own collections under local stewardship.

questions: is the museum only in english
can i contribute in another language
entries.answer: English is currently the source edition. Browser translation is available for now. Future translations should identify the language used and keep local wording where it matters. Language stewardship is part of the Museum’s longer-term plan.

questions: does the site support keyboard navigation
can i use this with a keyboard
entries.answer: The site includes light, dark, and automatic color themes, keyboard focus states, a skip link, responsive layouts, and reduced-motion handling. Translation and broader accessibility work are still part of the Museum’s ongoing stewardship.

questions: what is this was somebody's tuesday
what can i see right now
entries.answer: The opening exhibition is “This Was Somebody’s Tuesday.” It’s in preparation and will reconstruct an ordinary day through alarms, kitchens, commutes, work, purchases, waiting, messages, errands, meals, screens, and sleep. The image area is intentionally waiting for an original photograph from the 2026 collection.

questions: is this museum still being built
entries.answer: The archive is open and the collection is actively forming. The current collection window is 2026 to the present.

questions: is there a real building i can visit
is there a museum building i can go to
can i go to the museum in person
where is this place in real life
entries.answer: For now, the Museum is here online and wherever ordinary life is being documented. The main Museum is currently a distributed digital archive rather than a public building.

questions: is there an organization behind it
entries.answer: The Museum was established in 2026 and is currently stewarded as an independent experimental cultural project. It isn’t yet a conventional museum organization, and its longer-term model is distributed stewardship.

questions: why does the museum talk about ai
why is there a data and ai section
what does data and ai mean
can the collection become a dataset
entries.answer: As the collection grows, it can also function as a dataset about human life. That’s why the Museum records permissions now instead of treating future data use as automatic. Public display, research, machine learning, and generative reuse are separate choices.

questions: how is this related to no one noticed
is this part of a novel
what is the speculative fiction project
why is there a future site
entries.answer: The Museum is real, and it’s also an institution imagined inside No One Noticed, a speculative fiction project. The project’s “Reality Layer” builds pieces of that imagined future in the present. The Museum begins collecting now instead of inventing a future historical collection later.

questions: is this related to the museum of everyday life
what is museum of everyday life
did you copy museum of everyday life
who is the museum of everyday life
entries.answer: The Museum of Everyday Life in Glover, Vermont is a related project that explores people and their relationships to everyday objects. This Museum was established before its stewards discovered that project. The similar names weren’t intentional, and the overlap is acknowledged on the About page.

questions: how do i contact the museum

entries.answer: The site provides email links for contributions and stewardship. The complete addresses are reconstructed in the browser to reduce simple address scraping.

questions: why is the email hidden in source
how do your email links work
why can i not see the email address in html
entries.answer: The site stores the visible email parts in reversed form and reconstructs the address in the browser. That reduces harvesting by simple scrapers, but it isn’t a guarantee against bots that execute JavaScript or infer the address.
